strengths: The paper addresses a relevant PEFT problem and proposes a simple, implementable modification: adding a query-dependent nonlinear projection to the attention output without extending the prefix sequence.
Table 1 reports substantial improvements across two models and three classification tasks: approximately 8.1 percentage points over LoRA and 29.4 over prefix-tuning on average.

The evaluation extends beyond classification to Banking77 transfer and alignment with SFT, DPO, and SimPO on 10,000 examples. Attention visualizations and representation analyses provide useful exploratory diagnostics.
weaknesses: The central causal explanation is not established. Prefix attention mass depends on learned logits, not simply relative sequence lengths. The paper does not measure this mass, systematically vary input length, or isolate normalization competition while holding other architectural choices fixed. Changes in deep-layer attention do not invalidate a fixed-input, single-layer restriction, and representation CKA is not a direct measure of attention patterns.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to adapters and existing attention-based PEFT methods. The final module, ELU(q)M, is effectively a nonlinear residual adapter with a frozen input projection. Comparisons against parallel adapters and separately normalized or gated prefix branches are necessary to show what the prefix-derived construction contributes. The analysis also assumes tied projected prefix keys and values, whereas standard prefix-tuning can parameterize layerwise keys and values independently.

Several derivation steps are heuristic rather than justified equivalences. Replacing the input-dependent mixing coefficient with a constant changes the model; removing the denominator changes it again. Layer normalization does not generally absorb scaling of an attention branch inside a residual transformer. Moreover, ELU features are not shown to approximate the exponential similarity kernel. Claims of expressivity matching full fine-tuning are unsupported.

Baseline fairness is unresolved. All methods use a learning rate of 2e-5 and 4,000 steps on extremely small datasets, without method-specific tuning or a documented validation-based stopping rule. This can affect prefix-tuning and full fine-tuning very differently. Exact trainable parameter counts and LoRA target modules are absent, so the claimed budget matching cannot be verified.

The experimental protocol is internally inconsistent. Section 6.1 describes five independent one-example-per-class rounds whose results are averaged, whereas Section 6.4 describes progressively increasing training sets. Table 1 values match the fifth-round endpoints in the plots, making the reported aggregation unclear. No standard deviations or confidence intervals are provided despite substantial few-shot sampling sensitivity.

The expressivity evidence is weak and partly conflicts with its interpretation. Figure 3 shows the PT+ spectrum dropping sharply around component 15 and falling below PT thereafter, rather than consistently decaying more slowly. Appendix B.1 measures final-layer differences between separately executed models, which include accumulated upstream changes rather than isolating the added bias. Neither this spectrum nor CKA establishes greater functional expressivity.

The broader empirical claims exceed the evidence. Banking77 transfer alone does not establish general OOD robustness, and comparing LLaMA2 with Qwen cannot isolate the effect of GQA from model size, pretraining, and other architectural differences. Table 2 reports only win-rate improvements, without absolute scores, uncertainty, or sufficient evaluator details; the advantages over LoRA are only 0.27–1.14 points.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are incomplete. Matrix dimensions, initialization, head sharing, precise module placement, prompt templates, label processing, and checkpoint selection are insufficiently specified. No measured memory, throughput, or inference-latency results substantiate the efficiency claims. These gaps, together with missing component ablations, prevent the promising results from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a relevant PEFT problem with a simple implementation: adding a query-dependent nonlinear projection to the attention output avoids competition between prefix and input tokens within a shared softmax.
Table 1 reports substantial improvements over standard prefix tuning and consistent improvements over LoRA across six model–dataset settings, averaging approximately 8.1 percentage points over LoRA.
Includes two model families, evaluation of retained performance on Banking77, and preliminary alignment experiments with SFT, DPO, and SimPO on 10,000 examples each.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established. Prefix attention mass depends on learned attention logits, not simply relative sequence lengths. The paper does not directly measure this mass against performance, systematically vary input length, or isolate decoupled normalization from the other architectural changes. Representation shifts and selected attention heatmaps do not demonstrate that the proposed tradeoff causes prefix tuning’s poor performance.

Novelty relative to nonlinear and parallel adapters is insufficiently established. The final update, ELU(q)M, is effectively an adapter with a frozen input projection. Comparisons against parameter-matched adapters and independently normalized or gated prefix attention are needed to determine whether the contribution extends beyond a useful architectural variant.

The derivation contains unsupported transitions. Replacing the input-dependent mixing coefficient with a constant changes the model rather than algebraically decomposing standard prefix tuning. Absorbing the coefficient through layer normalization is not generally exact in a transformer with residual connections. The ELU feature map is not justified as an approximation to the exponential similarity kernel, and removing the denominator is a further heuristic requiring ablation.

The expressivity evidence is problematic. Figure 3 shows the Prefix-Tuning+ spectrum dropping sharply around component 15 and falling below the prefix-tuning spectrum, contrary to the text’s claim of slower decay and broader dimensional coverage. Appendix B measures differences between final-layer outputs, which include propagated changes from earlier layers rather than isolating the added bias. Likewise, decoder-output CKA is not a direct measure of attention-pattern changes or expressive capacity.

Baseline optimization is insufficiently validated. All methods use 4,000 steps, batch size 2, and a constant learning rate of 2e-5 despite the extremely small training sets and different optimization requirements. No method-specific tuning or validation-based checkpoint selection is described. The exceptionally weak prefix-tuning results therefore need stronger controls before supporting broad conclusions.

The training protocol is internally inconsistent. Section 6.1 describes five independent one-example-per-class rounds with results averaged across rounds, while Section 6.4 describes incrementally increasing training data. Table 1’s BigBench values match the fifth-round values in Figure 5 rather than the average of its displayed rounds. Missing uncertainty estimates make this ambiguity particularly consequential.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are incomplete: the manuscript does not adequately specify the dimensions, initialization, and head-sharing arrangement of M, LoRA target modules and scaling, exact parameter counts, prompts, or handling of multilabel GoEmotions examples. No measured memory, latency, or training-cost comparisons substantiate the efficiency claims.

The breadth and interpretation of evaluation are overstated. BigBench denotes only Date Understanding; differences between LLaMA2 and Qwen cannot isolate the effect of GQA. Banking77 measures cross-task performance retention without establishing beneficial transfer. Alignment gains over LoRA are only 0.27–1.14 points, with no uncertainty estimates, absolute win rates, or sufficiently detailed AlpacaEval configuration. These promising results do not resolve the methodological gaps required for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: improving prefix-based adaptation of modern language models. The proposed additive query-dependent module is simple and potentially useful.
Table 1 reports improvements over LoRA in all six model–dataset settings, averaging approximately 8.1 percentage points, and substantial gains over standard prefix-tuning.

Experiments cover two model families, three classification tasks, retention on Banking77, and larger-data alignment with SFT, DPO, and SimPO. This provides encouraging preliminary evidence beyond a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The central causal explanation is not established. Attention mass depends on learned similarity scores, not merely relative sequence lengths. There are no controlled input-length experiments, direct measurements of prefix attention mass, or ablations separating externalization, kernel replacement, and normalization removal. Representation changes alone do not demonstrate that prefix–input competition causes poor performance.

Figure 3 appears to contradict its interpretation: the Prefix-Tuning+ spectrum drops more sharply and has a substantially smaller tail than standard prefix-tuning, whereas the text claims slower decay and a more diverse subspace. Moreover, final-layer representation differences include effects propagated through the entire network, so they do not directly measure the expressivity of the local prefix module. Likewise, decoder-representation CKA is not a direct measure of attention-pattern changes.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to adapter methods. Equation (8) is an additive nonlinear transformation of frozen query features with a trainable output matrix. The paper needs explicit positioning and parameter-matched comparisons against parallel adapters and related attention adapters to establish the contribution beyond its prefix-tuning motivation.

The evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent. Section 6.1 describes five independent one-example-per-class runs whose results are averaged, while Section 6.4 describes incrementally increasing training data. Table 1 values match the fifth-round results in the figures. This leaves the actual sample budget and averaging procedure unclear. No standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported.

Baseline optimization and reproducibility are inadequate. All methods receive the same learning rate and 4,000 steps despite very different optimization requirements and extremely small training sets. There is no method-specific tuning or clear validation/checkpoint-selection protocol. Exact parameter counts, LoRA target modules and scaling, and PT+ matrix dimensions, initialization, and head sharing are missing. Runtime and memory savings are also not measured.

Several derivation steps are heuristic but presented too strongly. A fixed mixing coefficient changes standard prefix attention rather than exactly decomposing it; absorbing that coefficient through layer normalization is not generally justified in a residual transformer. Plain ELU is not established as an approximation to the exponential attention kernel, and removing the denominator further breaks that interpretation. Claims of expressivity matching full fine-tuning are unsupported.

The broader conclusions exceed the evidence. Banking77 primarily tests retention or cross-task transfer, rather than distribution shift within the trained task. Comparing LLaMA2-7B with Qwen2.5-3B cannot isolate GQA effects. Alignment improvements over LoRA are only 0.27–1.14 percentage points, without absolute scores, uncertainty, or sufficient evaluator details. These unresolved issues prevent the promising results from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a relevant question: whether prefix-based adaptation can remain competitive on modern LLMs. The proposed additive, query-conditioned module is simple and potentially practical.
Reports substantial improvements over vanilla Prefix-Tuning across two model families and three classification tasks, with additional encouraging results on preference alignment and math reasoning.
Includes useful supplementary analyses of LoRA ranks, feature-map choices, parameter counts, training throughput, inference latency, and retention of performance on an unrelated task.
weaknesses: The central causal diagnosis is not established. The softmax decomposition demonstrates competition between prefix and input contributions, but does not show that this is the primary cause of poor adaptation. Attention mass depends on learned logits as well as sequence lengths. There are no controlled input-length experiments, direct measurements of prefix attention mass, or ablations separating normalization decoupling from increased capacity and changed parameterization. Representation CKA is not a direct measure of attention patterns, even when only attention-module parameters are trained.

Novelty is insufficiently distinguished from existing adapter and memory approaches. The final method adds a nonlinear transformation of frozen queries followed by a trainable linear map, making comparisons with parallel adapters and closely related external-memory methods particularly important. The experiments mainly compare against vanilla Prefix-Tuning and LoRA; they do not establish what is gained specifically by the proposed prefix-memory interpretation.

The derivation mixes architectural changes with mathematical equivalences. Equation 4 is not an exact decomposition of Equation 2 when the mixing coefficient is fixed. Absorbing the scaling of the frozen attention branch into trainable weights and layer normalization is not generally justified in a residual transformer. Removing the query-dependent denominator is another substantive change. These may be reasonable design decisions, but their effects require ablation rather than an approximation narrative alone.

Figure 3 does not support the stated expressivity argument. The PMT spectrum drops sharply around component 15 and lies below Prefix-Tuning thereafter, whereas the text claims slower decay and a more broadly distributed representation. Moreover, Appendix B.1 measures differences between final-layer outputs of separately adapted networks, which include propagated upstream changes rather than isolating the additive module. A normalized effective-rank analysis with matched budgets would be more informative.

Baseline tuning and parameter matching are unclear. The reported common learning rate of 2e-5 and 4,000 steps on extremely small training sets do not demonstrate that each method was appropriately optimized. The main setup specifies LoRA rank 64, but Table 1 values match the rank-32 results in Table 7 after rounding. Table 8 also shows that PMT is closer to rank 32 than rank 64 in parameter count. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in comparison fairness.

The few-shot evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent. Sections 6.1 and A.1 describe averages over five independent trials, while Figure 5 and Appendix A.3 describe incrementally increasing training sets. Table 1's BigBench results match the fifth-round values plotted in Figure 5, leaving unclear whether they are trial averages or final-round measurements. No variability estimates are supplied. Furthermore, 'BigBench' denotes only Date Understanding, substantially narrowing the apparent benchmark coverage.

The application-scale results lack sufficient reproducibility and statistical support. AlpacaEval reports only win-rate deltas, without absolute scores, uncertainty, or a clear length-control specification. Math evaluation lacks detailed decoding, answer extraction, and repeated-run information; several AMC/AIME gains correspond to only a few questions. The unusually large Minerva-Math improvement warrants stronger validation. Essential implementation details, including memory initialization, head sharing, positional-encoding placement, and task-specific training settings, are also insufficiently specified.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. Comparing different model families and sizes does not isolate a benefit from GQA. Banking77 evaluation primarily measures cross-task retention rather than demonstrating general OOD robustness. Inference measurements omit merged LoRA, a crucial deployment baseline, and PMT is slower than both the base model and Prefix-Tuning on the reported 7B decoding measurements.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: improving prefix-based adaptation of modern LLMs. The proposed additive query-conditioned module is simple and potentially practical.

Reported results are promising across few-shot classification, preference alignment, and math reasoning. Table 1 shows substantial improvements over prefix-tuning, and Table 3 reports sizeable gains over LoRA.
The evaluation includes two model families, several training objectives, LoRA rank comparisons, and measurements of memory, throughput, and inference latency.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established. Softmax competition is a plausible limitation, but attention visualizations and representation CKA do not demonstrate that it causes poor downstream performance. There are no controlled input-length experiments, direct measurements of prefix attention mass, or ablations separating externalization from increased capacity and removal of normalization. Prefix attention mass also depends on learned logits, not simply relative sequence lengths.

The derivation overstates equivalence. Equation 4 replaces the input-dependent mixture in Equation 3 with a constant coefficient, changing the model rather than merely splitting its computation. Absorbing the coefficient on frozen attention into trainable weights and layer normalization is not generally exact within a residual transformer. Removing the query-dependent denominator is another substantive architectural change. These steps need explicit justification or controlled empirical validation.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to parallel adapters and related additive memory modules. The final update, phi(q)^T M, is a nonlinear feature transformation followed by a trainable projection. Comparisons against parameter-matched adapters, a linear-feature variant, and separately normalized prefix attention would clarify whether the contribution extends beyond this familiar construction.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility remain uncertain. Appendix C reports a common learning rate of 2e-5 without method-specific tuning evidence, while the few-shot protocol uses 4,000 steps on extremely small training sets. More concretely, the main text identifies LoRA as rank 64, but its Table 1 results closely match the rank-32 results in Table 7; Table 8 also contradicts the claim that rank 64 approximately matches PMT's parameter budget. These inconsistencies need resolution.

The expressivity evidence is problematic. Figure 3's PMT spectrum drops sharply around component 22 and subsequently lies below the prefix-tuning spectrum, which does not straightforwardly support the stated slower-decay interpretation. Appendix B.1 measures final-layer output differences between separately adapted models, rather than isolating the added bias at a shared input. Consequently, the spectrum confounds accumulated representation changes with the module's intrinsic expressivity.

Statistical support is inadequate. Although five trials are described for classification, no standard deviations or confidence intervals are reported. Preference alignment reports only win-rate deltas, without absolute scores, uncertainty, or clear length-control details. Math results lack repeated-run uncertainty, especially relevant for small benchmarks such as AIME24, and the unusually large Minerva-Math improvement warrants stronger verification.

Several conclusions exceed the evaluation. 'BigBench' is only Date Understanding; Banking77 measures transfer to one different task rather than broad OOD robustness. Attributing larger gains to GQA confounds architecture with model family, size, and pretraining. The application-scale experiments compare primarily against LoRA, leaving the claimed modernization of prefix-tuning less directly tested in those settings.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: whether prefix-based adaptation can remain competitive on modern LLMs. The proposed additive, query-conditioned memory module is simple and potentially useful.

Reported classification results are encouraging: PMT substantially improves over prefix-tuning and exceeds LoRA across all six model–dataset settings in Table 1. Comparisons with LoRA+, multiple LoRA ranks, and full fine-tuning provide useful context.
Evaluation extends beyond few-shot classification to preference optimization and mathematical reasoning. The reported Minerva-Math improvement at 50K training examples is particularly substantial.
The paper reports parameter counts, training throughput, memory usage, and inference latency, providing some evidence of practical feasibility.
weaknesses: The central causal explanation is insufficiently established. Prefix attention mass depends on learned logits, not simply relative sequence lengths. There is no controlled input-length experiment or direct measurement linking prefix mass to performance, and no ablation that separates externalizing softmax normalization from replacing prefixes with an unrestricted matrix. Representation CKA and selected attention heatmaps do not establish that normalization competition causes prefix-tuning's poor performance.

The expressivity evidence is problematic. Figure 3 shows PMT's spectrum dropping sharply around component 15 and falling below prefix-tuning thereafter, contrary to the accompanying claim of slower decay and broader principal-component coverage. Moreover, Appendix B.1 measures differences between final-layer outputs of separately adapted networks, rather than isolating the additive prefix module. These measurements do not establish the claimed module-level expressivity advantage.

Novelty relative to existing adapters is inadequately established. The final update, phi(q)M, is a nonlinear residual adapter operating on a frozen query projection. The paper does not compare against closely related parallel adapters or disentangled/gated prefix variants, while cited context-based methods such as DePT and ADePT are absent from experiments. The connection to prefix-tuning is motivational, but a distinct architectural contribution remains insufficiently demonstrated.

The mathematical construction contains unjustified transitions. Equation 4 substitutes a constant mixing coefficient for an input-dependent quantity, so it is an architectural change rather than an equivalent split. Absorbing the coefficient on the frozen attention branch through layer normalization is not generally valid in a residual transformer, and removing the query-dependent denominator is another substantive change. Additionally, the shared-prefix-vector formulation does not cover common prefix implementations with independently parameterized keys and values, weakening the claimed generality of the competing-optimization argument.

Baseline tuning and statistical reliability are insufficiently documented. Appendix C gives one learning rate, while the diagnostic experiments train on only 6–28 examples for 4,000 steps; appropriate method-specific learning rates and checkpoint selection are therefore crucial. Five-trial averages are reported without variability. Preference-alignment advantages over LoRA are only 0.27–1.14 percentage points, with no uncertainty estimates, absolute win rates, or clear length-control specification. The larger-scale experiments also omit prefix-tuning and other close alternatives.

The experimental protocol contains material inconsistencies. Section 6.1 and Appendix A.1 describe independent one-example-per-class trials averaged together, whereas Figures 5, 8, and 9 describe incrementally increasing training data; Table 1 values match the plotted fifth-round endpoints. The main LoRA baseline is labeled rank 64, but its Table 1 results closely match the rank-32 results in Table 7. Table 2 includes an MLP kernel despite the text describing MLP evaluation as future work. These discrepancies make the reported comparisons difficult to interpret and reproduce.

Important implementation and claim-support details remain missing. The multi-head/GQA parameterization and initialization of M, LoRA target modules, evaluation prompts, and application-specific training and decoding settings are not sufficiently specified. Comparing LLaMA2-7B with Qwen2.5-3B cannot isolate benefits attributable to GQA because model family, size, and pretraining also differ. Overall, the promising numerical results do not yet overcome the unresolved mechanistic, comparative, and reproducibility weaknesses required for acceptance.
